policy: research authoring index only; not runtime admission; final Wave-1500 consolidation required

waves.focus: 2026 scoping review mapped 22 trials of supplemental glycine/collagen; all three glycine sleep trials reported at least one favorable sleep outcome, but collagen-to-glycine mediation has not been directly tested and efficacy evidence remains small/mechanistic.

Eight-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in 45 medication-naive children with ADHD/subthreshold symptoms; the higher-dose phosphatidylserine plus DHA arm improved selected attention, impulsivity, hyperactivity, reaction-time and Stroop outcomes, but DHA/formulation and pediatric-context boundaries prevent phosphatidylserine-only attribution.

Four-arm randomized triple-masked trial in 97 professional male football players; taurine+caffeine+phosphatidylserine combinations improved selected cognitive, psychomotor, sprint and locomotor outcomes, but the multi-ingredient design prevents phosphatidylserine-specific attribution and fatigue-resistance change was not established from baseline.

2026 human-evidence review summarizes small cognition, stress/anxiety and sleep-quality signals from randomized evidence, often stronger with caffeine; dose-range summaries are study exposures rather than consumer dosing guidance and heterogeneity/interaction uncertainty remain.

Thirteen-RCT meta-analysis in 561 adults age 50+ found no additional benefit of HMB plus resistance training for fat mass, muscle mass or muscle strength; direct null counterweight to routine HMB adjunct claims in exercisable older adults.

Seven-RCT sarcopenia meta-analysis found strength-training plus supplementation improved several functional/body-composition outcomes overall, but subgroup benefit was clearer for whey protein than HMB; combined-intervention evidence cannot be assigned to HMB alone.

Nine-RCT/496-participant sarcopenia meta-analysis found low-to-very-low-certainty improvements in handgrip, gait speed and physical-performance measures when amino-acid-based supplements were added to resistance training, with no clear muscle-mass benefit and substantial intervention heterogeneity.

Systematic review of recurrent-UTI prevention in women found therapy-specific differences: methenamine and vaginal estrogen had stronger support, while D-mannose and cranberry showed mixed efficacy; category evidence must not be collapsed into a generic supplement claim.

Sixteen-study/1,171-participant meta-analysis found no significant overall effect of fenugreek on ALT, AST or ALP; an ALP subgroup signal at higher studied exposures does not overturn the overall liver-enzyme null and is not dosing guidance.

Thirteen randomized placebo-controlled trials in adult men found a small total-testosterone signal but no stable free-testosterone benefit; all primary evidence was very low certainty and the authors rejected clinical/commercial testosterone-boosting claims.

Systematic review of six human studies found cautiously positive adjunctive signals for pain/function/imaging after tendon or ligament injury/repair, but evidence was sparse, heterogeneous, low certainty and many oral interventions were multicomponent.

Seven-RCT/188-participant meta-analysis found lower advanced oxidation protein products after exercise but no significant changes in several other oxidative, inflammatory or muscle-injury biomarkers; broader physiological/performance benefit remains unconfirmed.

Twenty-four-RCT meta-analysis found lower creatine kinase and LDH with astaxanthin but no significant improvement in VO2max, time-trial performance or maximal workload/power; recovery-biomarker signals remain distinct from performance efficacy.

Twenty-two-RCT/822-participant review pooled Spirulina, Chlorella, brown-algal polysaccharides and astaxanthin; selected aerobic/recovery signals were species-, dose- and training-context dependent, so the evidence remains category-level rather than transferable across algae products.

Systematic review of 11 controlled trials across ADHD and adult mental disorders found heterogeneous, inconsistent cognitive effects; current evidence did not support citicoline or phosphatidylserine-containing compounds as established cognitive enhancers.

Eight-RCT meta-analysis found a small reduction in CRP with Spirulina but no significant TNF-alpha or IL-6 effect, with significant heterogeneity; this supports a narrow biomarker statement rather than a broad anti-inflammatory claim.

Eighteen-RCT/1,023-participant diabetes meta-analysis found improved insulin-resistance and selected inflammatory/oxidative biomarkers, while LDL cholesterol increased modestly; disease-specific surrogate outcomes and mixed lipid direction remain explicit.

Twelve-RCT/3,350-participant meta-analysis in healthy working adults found a small pooled improvement in subclinical depression/anxiety/stress symptoms and lower cortisol, with no CRP effect and insufficient sleep evidence; strain/dose/duration heterogeneity remains substantial.

Six-RCT/341-participant meta-analysis of probiotic monotherapy in unmedicated depression found a small symptom benefit, but sensitivity analysis excluding industry-funded/adjunctive-agent studies became nonsignificant; formulation and funding-bias boundaries are first-class.

Forty-one-RCT meta-analysis found a modest cortisol reduction with probiotics, but heterogeneity was extreme and GRADE certainty very low; subgroup strain patterns and exposure ranges are not optimization guidance.

Network meta-analysis of 38 RCTs in major depression found signals across microbiota-based therapies, prebiotics and probiotic categories, but certainty was low-to-moderate and network rankings do not establish superiority of a specific strain or product.

Ten-RCT/486-participant meta-analysis in depression found lower CRP and TNF-alpha with probiotic supplementation, borderline IL-1beta change, and null IL-6/IL-10; biomarker findings remain distinct from antidepressant efficacy and strain-specific attribution.

Twenty-three-RCT/1,005-participant meta-analysis in overweight/obesity found no significant effect on body weight, BMI, fat mass, body-fat percentage, fat-free mass, waist-hip ratio, adiponectin or leptin, with only waist circumference significantly reduced overall.

Umbrella review of 45 systematic reviews covering 129 associations found only four high-certainty positive associations, including waist circumference and selected lipid/BP outcomes in specific populations; most health claims remain lower-certainty and population-specific.

Twelve double-blind placebo-controlled exercise trials found no significant IL-6 or malondialdehyde effect and a CRP reduction based on only two small trials; overall recovery biomarker evidence was low-to-very-low certainty and hypothesis-generating.

Pooled meta-analysis of four randomized placebo-controlled dementia trials (488 patients) with prior cerebral infarction found statistically significant benefits for cognition, activities of daily living and global clinical impression with proprietary EGb 761; subgroup/proprietary-extract boundaries remain explicit.

Systematic review of seven rheumatic-disease studies found promising symptom/inflammatory signals in rheumatoid and osteoarthritis populations, but overall certainty was low to very low because of small samples, heterogeneous preparations and short follow-up.

Forty-one-RCT systematic review found pooled improvements in several glycemic, lipid, blood-pressure and inflammatory biomarkers, while multiple other outcomes were null; surrogate-endpoint and baseline-risk modifiers remain explicit.

Thirteen-trial type-2-diabetes meta-analysis found statistically significant fasting-glucose, HbA1c, systolic-BP, triglyceride and HDL changes, but HOMA-IR, diastolic BP, total cholesterol, LDL and BMI were null and effect magnitudes were often of limited clinical importance.

GRADE-based 12-RCT blood-pressure meta-analysis found modest SBP/DBP reductions with ginger but rated certainty low because of inconsistency, short duration and limited robustness; dose-response subgroup findings are study evidence rather than dosing guidance.

Network meta-analysis of randomized trials in healthy aging/MCI found domain-specific signals for several nutrient combinations and single nutrients, but rankings were sensitive to sample size/duration and the heterogeneous interventions prevent ingredient-level equivalence claims.

Cochrane review of 16 randomized trials (4,083 children) evaluated oral vitamin B12 for growth, development and cognition; outcomes varied by endpoint and trial context, requiring age, baseline-status, co-nutrient and duration boundaries rather than a universal pediatric cognition claim.

Thirty-one-RCT glycemic meta-analysis found no significant fasting-glucose reduction with melatonin, while HbA1c, fasting-insulin and HOMA-IR signals improved; fasting-glucose null and metabolic-population boundaries remain first-class.

Twelve-trial/1,977-participant cancer-fatigue meta-analysis found a pooled fatigue reduction but very low GRADE certainty and substantial heterogeneity; apparent exposure/duration patterns are not converted into consumer dosing guidance.

Five randomized trials (323 hemodialysis patients) found improved PSQI and selected sleep domains with melatonin; the disease-specific evidence remains limited in certainty and should not be generalized to primary insomnia.

Five RCTs/561 breast-cancer radiotherapy patients found less fatigue and improvements in cognitive/global-health measures, with several emotional, social, physical, gastrointestinal, pain and sleep domains null; small samples and heterogeneous regimens limit inference.

Seven randomized IBS trials (391 adults) found improvements in overall symptom severity, pain frequency and defecation frequency, while quality of life and global sleep quality were not significantly improved; short-term IBS-specific evidence only.

Systematic/ethnobotanical review found historical abortifacient claims vulnerable to citation distortion and available animal/human data did not establish significant teratogenic or abortifacient activity; absence of robust pregnancy-specific controlled evidence keeps reproductive-safety conclusions incomplete.

GRADE-assessed meta-analysis of 34 RCTs/1,769 adults found improvements on self-reported BDI/BAI scores but no significant HDRS, HARS or POMS effects; high heterogeneity and discordance between self- and clinician-rated outcomes constrain broad antidepressant/anxiolytic claims.

Eight RCTs in adult male soccer players found inconsistent biomarker/functional recovery effects, with more favorable soreness/well-being trends in selected tart-cherry, beetroot and curcumin studies; certainty was low or very low and remains category-level.

Systematic review of 14 black-cohosh clinical-trial reports found wide variation in CONSORT herbal-intervention and harms-reporting quality; the review chiefly informs evidence quality and adverse-event reporting rather than establishing efficacy.

International Menopause Society evidence update reviewed 158 studies and found most complementary-therapy evidence low/very-low certainty, with moderate-certainty support for selected black-cohosh/CHM/acupuncture combinations and vitamin-D outcomes; broad category evidence only.

Thirty-RCT review of 19 non-soy herbal interventions found substantial heterogeneity; most studies reported some symptom improvement but black cohosh and dong quai trials included null findings, preventing a class-wide efficacy conclusion.

Updated meta-analysis of 108 RCTs/7,137 adults found modest pooled improvements across several lipid, glycemic, blood-pressure, inflammatory and oxidative biomarkers, while ApoA1/ApoB, ALT, IL-6, BMI, weight and adiponectin were null; surrogate-outcome boundaries retained.

2026 retraction notice for a prior aged-garlic-extract blood-pressure meta-analysis; downstream evidence systems must quarantine the retracted synthesis and preserve retraction provenance rather than continuing to cite its pooled estimate.

Seven-RCT review of vitamin D and vitamins C/E in endometriosis reported selected pain/oxidative-stress signals but no significant pregnancy-rate improvement; multiple vitamins and heterogeneous regimens make this category-level adjunctive evidence.

Twelve-RCT MASLD meta-analysis found a triglyceride reduction with vitamin E but no significant overall total-cholesterol, LDL, HDL or BMI change; disease-specific lipid evidence is mixed and largely surrogate.

Systematic review of nine pediatric dialysis studies (194 patients) found limited, outcome-specific signals for hemoglobin/ESA use and cardiac function, with several lipid/inflammatory/QoL outcomes null; small heterogeneous evidence base limits pediatric inference.

Systematic review across mechanistic and clinical CAD evidence reported possible inflammatory/oxidative and selected clinical signals, but heart-failure and reinfarction results were inconsistent; mixed study designs prevent a high-certainty treatment claim.

Systematic review of clinical and experimental poisoning evidence found toxin-specific, mostly adjunctive signals for L-carnitine/acetyl-L-carnitine, with no basis to replace established antidotes/supportive care; heterogeneous toxins and mixed human/preclinical evidence require category-level handling.

New Zealand general-population analysis found substantial concurrent natural-health-product and medicine use, including potential interactions involving fish oil, coenzyme Q10, turmeric and glucosamine; one fish-oil/warfarin combination was rated potentially significant, and coding of supplement exposures was often incomplete.

Systematic review of melatonin use in children age 0-6 found rising prescribing, extended use and overdose exposures; short trials in neurologic conditions suggested sleep-onset benefit with few adverse events, but long-term outcomes and efficacy in typically developing young children were absent.

Umbrella review covering 52 reviews, 250 RCTs and 18 supplements found most evidence low/critically-low quality, with only selected moderate-certainty supportive-care benefits and dose-related or serious adverse events for some vitamins/minerals; broad category evidence only.

Twenty-study/1,737-participant GDM meta-analysis found improvements in glycemic markers and several pregnancy/neonatal outcomes with vitamin D, but substantial heterogeneity and methodological limitations make these exploratory disease-specific findings.

Pulmonary-tuberculosis meta-analysis found higher sputum-smear conversion and fewer adverse events with adjunctive vitamin D but no significant culture-conversion benefit; outcome-specific certainty and route/duration heterogeneity prevent a broad TB-treatment claim.

Critical ASD review found inconsistent observational status data and mixed RCT results; only one high-dose trial showed broad symptom improvements while other trials were marginal/null, leading the authors to reject vitamin D as a general ASD-targeted intervention.

Umbrella review of 21 asthma syntheses found a possible exacerbation-risk reduction with vitamin D but inconsistent effects on symptom control, lung function and inflammatory outcomes; evidence certainty was frequently low/very low and primary-study overlap was substantial.

Eight-RCT/617-participant hemodialysis meta-analysis found lower CRP and iPTH and slightly higher albumin with nutritional vitamin D, with no significant increase in overall adverse reactions, hypercalcemia or hyperphosphatemia; dialysis-specific evidence only.

Systematic review of 11 high-dose vitamin-D RCTs in multiple sclerosis found serum-level and immunologic changes with rare transient calcium disturbances, but clinical and MRI benefits were inconsistent; high-dose safety conclusions require monitored trial context.

Umbrella review of nine tuberculosis systematic reviews found consistently null primary outcomes for culture conversion, time to conversion and mortality, with subgroup signals considered hypothesis-generating; strong counterweight to routine adjunctive vitamin-D claims in unselected TB.

Umbrella review in diabetic kidney disease found low-certainty reductions in surrogate urinary albumin/protein markers but no consistent benefit for eGFR, creatinine, kidney replacement therapy, mortality or cardiovascular events, with safety inadequately reported.

Systematic review of 10 prospective breast-cancer chemotherapy trials found inconsistent efficacy across DHA/EPA combinations with or without vitamin D/GLA, no consistent treatment-response or survival benefit, and low-to-very-low certainty; co-supplementation prevents ingredient-level attribution.

Structured sports-nutrition review identified highest contamination/ADRV risk in multi-ingredient pre-workouts, weight-loss, muscle-building and testosterone-boosting products and emphasized third-party certification, product verification and documentation; product-quality/safety infrastructure evidence only.

Five-year randomized Finnish trial in 2,495 largely vitamin-D-sufficient older adults found neither 1,600 nor 3,200 IU/day reduced fracture risk; the lower-dose arm had more fractures than placebo, directly arguing against high-dose fracture-prevention claims in replete populations.

Fourteen-study hemodialysis meta-analysis found modest hemoglobin/TSAT improvements and lower weight-adjusted ESA requirements with ascorbic acid, but certainty was low, heterogeneity high, and long-term safety/patient-centered outcomes unestablished.

Systematic review of nutritional antioxidants in breast cancer highlighted a double-edged interaction with therapy: selected supplements may reduce toxicities, while antioxidant use during oxidative cytotoxic treatment may theoretically or observationally compromise treatment effects; broad mechanistic/clinical category evidence.

Forensic systematic review/meta-analysis linked supplement contamination to a meaningful share of unintentional anti-doping violations and described cardiovascular risks from performance-enhancing substances; contamination estimates and nutrition alternatives remain sport-regulatory context rather than product efficacy evidence.

Systematic review of 44 empirical studies estimated roughly 9-15% of tested supplements contained prohibited or undeclared pharmacological substances, especially stimulants/anabolic agents in pre-workout, weight-loss and muscle-building products; product-integrity safety evidence only.

Systematic review of five adolescent/youth creatine studies found no consistent short-term renal, hepatic or cardiometabolic safety signals or serious attributed adverse events, but the evidence base was small and lacked long standardized follow-up.

Meta-analysis of 48 athlete studies found higher odds of headache, abdominal discomfort, tachycardia, insomnia, anxiety, nervousness and increased urination with acute caffeine, with several side effects increasing with dose; safety effects remain distinct from ergogenic benefit.

Systematic review/meta-analysis in adolescent athletes found only a small uncertain acute physical-performance benefit, sparse cognitive evidence and inconsistent adverse-event reporting; current evidence did not support routine caffeine use in youth sport.

Thirteen-study hemodialysis review found selected CRP reductions with omega-3 formulations but substantial heterogeneity and poor adverse-event reporting; reported events were mostly mild, while optimal formulation/composition remains uncertain.

Systematic review of recent Serenoa repens evidence found symptom improvements in some BPH/LUTS studies and generally favorable tolerability, but extract/formulation, combination-treatment and study-design heterogeneity substantially limited comparability.

Umbrella meta-analysis found dietary therapies such as low-glycemic-index treatment reduced seizure frequency while antioxidant adjuncts did not show significant efficacy; adverse events increased overall, especially with ketogenic diets, so this remains broad category evidence.

Six-RCT/438-participant septic-shock meta-analysis found lower in-hospital mortality and renal-replacement-therapy use with thiamin; critically ill population and treatment-context boundaries prevent extrapolation to general supplementation.

Meta-analysis of three adult RCTs found small reductions in stress and anxiety with bovine milk-fat-globule-membrane supplementation, while depression effects were nonsignificant; the evidence base is only three trials and remains preliminary.

Systematic review/meta-analysis found lower circulating short-chain fatty acids in depression and six RCTs suggested probiotic/prebiotic interventions can raise fecal SCFAs alongside symptom improvement; biomarker associations do not establish a specific supplement mechanism or strain effect.

Systematic review of 122 psychiatric nutraceutical studies found heterogeneous signals across vitamin D, NAC, acetyl-L-carnitine, CoQ10, alpha-lipoic acid, magnesium and B vitamins, with high overall risk of bias and low methodological quality; category-level evidence only.

Thirteen-RCT/710-participant meta-analysis in major depressive disorder found a small pooled symptom benefit favoring probiotics with moderate heterogeneity; strain/formulation uncertainty prevents generic probiotic equivalence.

Scoping review found very limited human mood evidence for gotu kola, phosphatidylcholine and taurine, with most supporting data preclinical and no studies of their combination; evidence is insufficient for quantitative synthesis or product-level claims.

Systematic review of 56 controlled human/animal studies found sleep-related signals from probiotics, prebiotics, dietary patterns and botanicals, but major intervention heterogeneity and mixed preclinical/human evidence prevent attribution to a single compound or strain.

Four-RCT schizophrenia meta-analysis found no significant effect on positive or total symptoms, a small low-certainty reduction in negative symptoms, and very uncertain effects on depression/general psychopathology; authors did not recommend clinical implementation.

Meta-analysis of 16 RCTs across curcumin, ascorbic acid, resveratrol and sulforaphane found non-robust and compound-specific schizophrenia signals; formulation/co-intervention heterogeneity and sparse data for several agents require category-level handling.

Network meta-analysis of 25 RCTs in PCOS found potential mood benefits for omega-3 plus vitamin E among several psychological/exercise/drug interventions, while vitamin D plus probiotics was not significantly beneficial; combined-intervention attribution firewall applies.

Four RCTs/1,342 women without diagnosed mental illness found limited strain-specific probiotic signals for perinatal depressive/anxiety symptoms; no prebiotic or synbiotic trials were available and risk of bias was moderate-to-high.

Systematic review of four probiotic studies in fibromyalgia found inconsistent anxiety/depression effects and insufficient safety reporting, so no definitive recommendation for or against probiotics could be made.

Systematic review of non-pharmacological/non-psychological depression augmentation found lower levels of evidence for probiotics than for exercise or bright-light approaches; augmentation evidence remains category-specific and does not establish probiotic monotherapy efficacy.

Systematic review of six prospective cohorts and four RCTs in IBD linked dysbiosis with anxiety/depression and found microbiota-targeted interventions sometimes improved symptoms, but interventions included probiotics and fecal microbiota transplantation and remained heterogeneous.

Meta-analysis of seven intervention RCTs found pooled depressive-symptom improvement from diverse SCFA-modulating strategies, including probiotics, FMT, vagal stimulation and direct butyrate; between-class differences were not significant and the evidence cannot be assigned to one supplement.

Nine-study/617-participant meta-analysis in MCI/Alzheimer/dementia found modest cognitive-score improvements with ginseng, but effects did not reach clear clinical significance and evidence was limited by small study count and heterogeneity.

Dose-response meta-analysis of observational studies associated higher dietary choline intake with lower risk of cognitive decline and Alzheimer-related outcomes, but this is non-randomized dietary evidence and cannot establish supplementation efficacy or an optimal supplemental dose.

Translational Parkinson review found consistent preclinical neuroprotection and small open-label human signals in UPDRS/DAT imaging, but randomized efficacy evidence was lacking; disease-modifying claims remain premature.

Seven placebo-controlled RCTs/566 participants found no consistent NAC benefit for alcohol craving or PTSD severity; a sensitivity-analysis signal emerged only after one study was removed, supporting an overall null/uncertain efficacy interpretation.

Meta-analysis of 74 RCTs found apparent adjunctive benefits for several anti-inflammatory agents including NAC and fatty acids, but publication bias, heterogeneity and sensitivity analyses weakened many effects; routine use was not robustly supported.

VaD-focused RCT meta-analysis found small cognitive effects for galantamine/memantine and a fragile very-low-certainty EGb 761 signal, while citicoline and several other interventions remained single-trial/non-poolable; patient-important benefits were uncertain.

Systematic review of eight acute RCTs/244 healthy participants found mostly null or small inconsistent taurine cognition/mood effects; more reliable benefits occurred in caffeine combinations that did not isolate taurine.

Small four-arm RCT in 36 peri/postmenopausal women found medium-dose creatine hydrochloride improved selected reaction-time, brain-creatine and lipid outcomes versus placebo, but sample size, formulation specificity and exploratory endpoints sharply limit generalization to creatine monohydrate.

Parallel trial in 40 young active adults found creatine monohydrate improved Wingate mean/peak power but did not improve Stroop or Trail cognitive outcomes; useful direct null evidence against broad acute cognition claims in healthy active adults.

Sleep-deprivation crossover trial in 29 healthy adults found a single creatine dose attenuated deterioration in several cognitive tasks during 21 hours of sleep loss; acute sleep-deprivation context and unusually large studied exposure prevent routine cognition/dosing extrapolation.

Meta-analysis of 16 pediatric ADHD RCTs found a small borderline overall PUFA benefit with stronger signals on performance-based cognition than subjective ratings; heterogeneity was substantial and PUFA supplementation was not supported as standalone treatment.
